name: SwiftDrome
subtitle: A SwiftUI client for Navidrome and Subsonic-API music servers.
description:
SwiftDrome is an iOS client for Subsonic-API-compatible music servers (primarily Navidrome), built with SwiftUI and Apple's Liquid Glass design language.

Log in to your own Navidrome/Subsonic server and browse your library: artists, albums, playlists, genres, and search. Stream playback with a queue engine that keeps a user-controlled "Play Next" stack separate from the main queue, plus favorites and back-skip history.

This source publishes unsigned .ipa builds automatically whenever a change is released, so the version here should always track the latest build.

apps.name: SwiftDrome
apps.subtitle: A SwiftUI client for Navidrome and Subsonic-API music servers.
apps.localizedDescription:
SwiftDrome is an iOS client for Subsonic-API-compatible music servers (primarily Navidrome), built with SwiftUI and Apple's Liquid Glass design language.

Log in to your own Navidrome/Subsonic server and browse your library: artists, albums, playlists, genres, and search. Stream playback with a queue engine that keeps a user-controlled "Play Next" stack separate from the main queue, plus favorites and back-skip history.

This .ipa is unsigned and built straight from the main branch, so it needs to be sideloaded (AltStore, SideStore, LiveContainer, etc.) rather than installed from the App Store.
apps.versionDescription: - The companion tries to push the album shelves on Home. With the home screen up, every so often it dives into the mini player, comes back out at the right edge of the screen and walks along the bottom of one of the album rows to the rightmost cover that is fully on screen, plants its paws on that cover's right edge and heaves against it three times over -- the whole row jolts a few points to the left under each shove, holds, and springs back the moment the pet gives up. It stands there for a beat looking at what it failed to move, then walks off the way it came and is thrown back out of the mini player. Which row it picks is random, so it doesn't develop a favourite. Scroll the row away or open the full player mid-push and the errand is abandoned rather than played to a screen that has moved on.

versions.localizedDescription: - The companion tries to push the album shelves on Home. With the home screen up, every so often it dives into the mini player, comes back out at the right edge of the screen and walks along the bottom of one of the album rows to the rightmost cover that is fully on screen, plants its paws on that cover's right edge and heaves against it three times over -- the whole row jolts a few points to the left under each shove, holds, and springs back the moment the pet gives up. It stands there for a beat looking at what it failed to move, then walks off the way it came and is thrown back out of the mini player. Which row it picks is random, so it doesn't develop a favourite. Scroll the row away or open the full player mid-push and the errand is abandoned rather than played to a screen that has moved on.

- Settings puts Storage right after Playback -- the two screens that matter while setting up streaming and downloads now sit together -- with Pets and Accessibility behind it. The playback-engine picker's summary is one line for both engines instead of changing with the choice, and the menu takes the width its labels need instead of hyphenating "Render (alpha)" mid-word.
- Playback Settings offers a second engine to play downloaded music with. "System player" is what SwiftDrome has always used and stays the default; "Render engine" is new, and it decodes downloaded songs in the app and hands them to an audio graph of its own, so the last sample of one song is followed by the first of the next with nothing at all in between. The old join was the closest thing the system's player has an API for -- close enough that most records sound continuous, and not close enough that a record mastered to run without a break always does. This one is not close: it is the same thing as no boundary. Songs already on the device play this way, and so do most songs still arriving over the network (the entry below says which); the two engines never sound at once.
- The render engine now plays songs that are still arriving over the network, off the same download the cache is keeping -- playback starts once a few seconds are on the device, and the boundary into the next downloaded song is the engine's own seamless join. This was the one place the engine still had the system player's audible gap: the moment a streamed song ended and a downloaded one began. It asks two things of the stream -- the server must send the file unchanged rather than transcoding it, and the format must be readable from its front, which FLAC, WAV and AIFF are; Opus and transcoded streams stay on the system player for now. Seeking inside a song that is still arriving hands that song to the system player, whose re-streamed seek lands exactly; a connection slower than the music pauses playback to buffer, the way a stream always has; and a stream the engine cannot start within a few seconds goes to the system player rather than being waited on in silence.
- The render engine streams transcoded music too: Opus, MP3 and FLAC transcodes play on it the same way untranscoded streams do, read as they arrive. A song delivered this way keeps the server's idea of its length rather than adopting the arriving file's guess, which for Ogg files has been wrong before. Two deliveries stay on the system player: AAC transcodes, whose file holds its table of contents until the end, and Ogg Vorbis, which the system cannot play at all.
- Seeking inside a song the render engine is streaming stays on the engine now. If the download has already finished in the background, the seek is served from the file on the device; a FLAC stream is rebuilt to start where the seek was aimed, landing inside a single frame -- the same machinery the system player has used for this; and a transcoded stream is asked for again starting at the target, with the fraction of a second the server cannot express decoded and dropped so the landing is exact. Before this, any seek in a streamed song quietly moved that song back to the system player for the rest of its runtime.
- Playback Settings ends with a small Debugging card holding one switch: "Download upcoming songs". It is on, and staying on is right for listening -- the lookahead is why album boundaries usually land between files already on the device. Turning it off makes every song stream as it starts, which is what testing streamed playback needs; downloads asked for by name still run.
- The new engine is worth calling experimental, and the picker says so. Two things it does not do yet: crossfading into a song that is not downloaded falls back to a plain gap between them, and two songs recorded at different sample rates are not joined to each other -- a boundary a record almost never has, since an album is one format throughout. Volume levelling, crossfading between downloaded songs, seeking, the lock screen and everything around them work as before. Anything the engine cannot take -- a surround recording, a file it cannot read -- is quietly handed back to the system player rather than failing.
- Seeking inside a downloaded song is exact under the new engine. It reads the file again from the frame the position names, where the system player works a position out from an assumed bitrate in some formats and lands somewhere else entirely -- the error SwiftDrome repacks downloaded FLACs to avoid. So is the length shown: the engine counted the song's frames to play them, rather than believing what the file claims about itself.
- The squirrel's flat-push animation got redrawn frames.

- The companion pays the play button a visit. With an album screen open, every so often it dives head-first into the mini player, turns up hauling itself over the top of the album's round play button, taps it three times with a paw -- the button dips under each tap, and nothing starts playing; the queue is yours, not the squirrel's -- then climbs back down behind the button and is thrown back out of the mini player it went into. It goes from wherever it happens to be: pacing the pill, sitting on its rim while the music is paused (it stands up first), or waiting inside the tab bar's collapsed capsule, in which case it slips off unseen and comes home to waiting there. If the button scrolls away or the full player opens mid-visit, the climb is abandoned rather than played to a screen that has moved on.
- Multi-disc albums play in the order they were released. Track numbers start again at 1 on every disc, and the on-device library was sorting an album by track number alone -- so a two-disc release came back interleaved, disc 1 track 1, disc 2 track 1, disc 1 track 2, and played that way. On a record meant to run continuously that is audible immediately: a remix from the second disc wedged between two songs written to follow each other. Worse, the two tracks either side of that wedge looked consecutive by number, so the player joined them gaplessly -- a hard butt-join between two pieces of music that have nothing to do with each other. Discs are now carried through from the server and the album is ordered by disc first.
- An album on more than one disc shows them as separate sections, headed "Disc 1", "Disc 2" and so on. Albums on a single disc are unchanged -- a lone "Disc 1" over every record would be a heading that says nothing -- and so are albums whose server doesn't report disc numbers.
- The seam where one disc ends and the next begins gets a plain gap: no crossfade, and no gapless join. That is the one place a release really is two records -- the side ran out, and whoever sequenced it knew you would get up and change it. Blending across it invents a continuity the record never had, and joining it removes a gap that is part of the work. Landing part-way into another disc, which is a shuffle's doing rather than the record's, still blends like any other pair.
- Updating re-fetches the library once. The disc numbers aren't in the copy already downloaded to the device and can't be worked out from what is -- they only ever existed in a response the sync had thrown away -- so the app asks the server for them again, as a full sync on the next launch. While it runs, the browse screens read from the server exactly as they do before a library has ever been downloaded, so albums are in the right order straight away rather than after the sync finishes.
- A library that was never fully downloaded now finishes the job on the next launch instead of never. The app only ever chose the full download for a completely empty library; anything else got the quick check, which looks at the newest albums and stops. A first download that was interrupted -- closed the app, lost the connection -- was therefore never resumed, and whatever it had not reached stayed missing however many times the app was opened. The quick check also asks the right question now: it used to look up which albums were still owed track lists by taking the first few hundred alphabetically and seeing whether any of the new albums were among them, which for most libraries they were not, so it concluded there was nothing to fetch.
- Editing the queue while one song is fading into the next now takes effect. A crossfade starts several seconds before a track ends and stays running -- and audible -- for the whole of that overlap, and anything done to the queue inside that window was ignored: taking out the song that was fading in, dragging another ahead of it, queueing something to play next, or pressing shuffle or repeat all left the blend running to its end. You heard several seconds of a song you had just removed, and only once the overlap finished did the player notice and jump to the right one. The queue is now read again the moment it changes, a blend aimed at a song that is no longer next is called off, and whatever really does come next is faded in instead -- the same check a gapless album join already got.
- The log tells the truth about shuffle, and about a crossfade that gets called off. The line reporting a new queue carried a "shuffling: true" that read as "shuffle is on" and was there for every ordinary play whether it was on or off; it now says "shuffle off", "shuffle on, shuffled as it landed", or -- for a queue picked up from another device, which keeps the order it arrived in -- "shuffle on, arriving order kept". A crossfade dropped part-way through by a skip, a seek or the queue moving under it used to leave no trace at all, so the only blends in the log were the ones that ran all the way to the end; one that is called off now says so, and how far it had got.
- The queue is choosier about what it gathers when it runs on past the end of what you started, and Playback has a "Skip short tracks" slider that says how choosy. Anything shorter than the length it is set to is taken for an interlude and left out; the default has moved from a minute to a minute and a half, and sliding it to zero turns the length test off altogether. Titles are read as well as lengths, and more carefully than before: a track called "Intro", "Outro", "Interlude" or "Skit" is left out, as is one that ends with that as an aside -- "Grace (Interlude)", "Grace [Skit 2]", "Grace -- Intro" -- while a song that merely contains the word is still a song, so "Intro to Reality", "The Outro Song" and "Skittles" stay. Only what the queue picks for itself is judged this way: an album or playlist you put on plays through whole, interludes included.
- The library can be browsed while it is being downloaded for the first time. Albums, artists, songs, genres, playlists and favourites are read from the on-device index once it has been filled once -- but a first full sync takes a while, and until it finished those screens had nothing to show and said so, on a connection that was working perfectly well. They now fetch from the server in the meantime, exactly as they did before there was an index at all, and switch over to the index the moment the sync completes. An album opened during that first sync arrives with its track list rather than empty, since track lists are the last thing a sync gathers.
- The Downloaded screen shows what is on the device while that first sync is still running. Downloaded files are stored by id alone, so each one is looked up for its title and artwork -- against the index when it has the song, against the server when it doesn't, which before the first sync finishes is every one of them. Those lookups all went out at once, queued behind the sync's own requests and timed out, and a lookup that failed took its row off the screen with it: a full set of downloads read as "nothing downloaded". They now go out a few at a time and each row appears as it resolves, and one that can't be looked up no longer removes the others.
- A small pixel-art companion now lives on top of the mini player: it wanders back and forth while music plays, and tapping it plays a quick crouch-jump-roll-land trick before it goes back to wandering. It hides along with the mini player itself while nothing is playing, while the full player is open, and while the mini player is minimized into the tab bar. Settings has a Pets screen for it: a switch to turn the companion off entirely, and the choice of which one keeps you company -- one to pick from today, shown animating in the list rather than just named.
- The companion on the mini player has more to do than pace. Stop the music and it walks to a halt, sits down on the rim of the pill and lets its legs hang over the edge; it gets up a beat after playback comes back, or straight away if you tap it, since a tap asked for the trick rather than for a get-up. Star what is playing and it turns and beats a heart -- every time the heart is pressed, on a song or on a whole album -- and while something you had already starred is playing it notices on its own now and again, at most once every forty seconds, so it stays company rather than a notification.
- Closing the full player hands the mini player a title that reads from its first word. The scrolling title and artist in the pill kept running the whole time the player was open, so the moment the player landed the line jumped to wherever the scroll had got to in the meantime -- often the middle of a word. Both lines now start their run over as the pill comes back.
- The companion leaves the mini player under its own steam when the tab bar folds the pill into its inline capsule. Instead of blinking out of existence, it turns to face the middle of the screen, gathers itself and dives for it, falls the gap down to wherever the row is on its way to, and disappears head-first through the edge of it. Whatever it was doing gives way to that -- a walk, a sit on the rim, a beat of the idle -- because the row it is standing on is already moving. Scroll back up before it has gone under and it breaks off the dive and carries on pacing; scroll back up after and it is standing where it went in.
- The companion has something to do while the mini player is folded away in the tab bar. Every so often it puts its head up over the edge of the collapsed pill for a look around -- somewhere new along it each time, since nothing could see where it went -- and ducks back in. Scroll the mini player back out and it waits for the pill to arrive back where it belongs before coming out of it, thrown up off the row and landing on its feet on top of it, as though the pill rising had flung it out.

- Music playing somewhere else can be picked up here. When another device is on a track -- the Navidrome web player in another room, a second phone, anything that reports to the server -- Home shows a banner naming it and what it is on, and Claim carries on from the second it had reached. Sessions that are paused are offered too, not only playing ones, since a paused session is exactly the one you walked away from. The other device keeps going: there is no way to pause another client over the Subsonic API, so this takes the session over rather than moving it, and the banner doesn't pretend otherwise. What comes across depends on what the other end published. Between two SwiftDrome devices the queue arrives with the track, once the device you are leaving has played something since it launched -- before that it has nothing published to hand over. From a client that never saves a play queue, and neither the Navidrome web player nor Supersonic ever does, there is no queue on the server to read: the track and its position transfer, and the banner says so before the tap rather than leaving it to be discovered afterwards. This device publishes its own session the same way, so the handoff works in both directions, and it runs whatever the scrobble setting says -- that setting governs play history alone. The banner can be dismissed, and pulling down to refresh Home brings it back if that session is still running; the app stops looking for sessions while it is in the background.
- With Left-Handed Controls on, the line under the artwork on the Now Playing screen mirrors: the year and genre move to the right, the heart and the ellipsis menu to the left, under the thumb. It is the same flip the album screen's action row already made, and only the two blocks swap sides -- the text inside each keeps its own reading order.
- AAC is still listed as a transcoding format but can no longer be picked. A server transcoding on the fly hands AAC over as ADTS, which carries nothing to say where the encoder's padding ends, so every track starts with about a twentieth of a second of silence that no amount of scheduling removes -- gapless playback is impossible in that format, not merely worse. The row stays in the menu, greyed, so the answer to "where did AAC go?" is on screen rather than absent, and anyone whose setting already reads AAC keeps it: what changed is that there is no way back to it.
- Each device registers with Navidrome under its own name. Since iOS 16 a device reports itself generically as "iPhone" unless an app asks Apple for the entitlement to read the real name, so two of the same phone arrived at the server as one player, each overwriting what the other was doing. The app now appends four characters unique to the install -- "SwiftDrome (iPhone·a1b2)" -- which is what shows up in Navidrome's Players list.

- The re-roll button on the home screen's random shelf answers the press properly. It turns once anticlockwise and coasts to a stop, then the arrow hands itself over to a checkmark -- the head fades off, the ring erases from its start until only the tail is left, and the check draws out of that tail -- before the whole thing runs backwards to the arrow again. A fresh shuffle can come back looking a lot like the one it replaced, so without that confirmation there is no telling a re-roll that worked from a button that did nothing; a re-roll that fails now ends on the plain arrow rather than claiming otherwise, and the button presses in under the finger straight away instead of waiting for the covers to arrive.
- Settings rows whose content is taller than an ordinary row -- a wrapped summary, a slider, a progress bar -- have room above and below again instead of sitting flush against the edge of the card, which read as the text hugging the bottom of the section. Rows of ordinary height are unchanged.

- The songs on the Downloaded screen answer to swipes like the songs on every other screen: right for Play Next, left for Play Last, and a long press for those plus starring and keeping. They had a long-press menu only, so a swipe that worked on an album or a playlist did nothing here.

- Closing the player lands on the mini player cleanly. The pill came home looking milky, because the shrinking player carried its own sheet of glass down onto the glass the tab bar was already drawing there -- two of them stacked for the whole way down. The player now drops its glass the moment it starts shrinking and lets the bar's own show through.
- The mini player no longer settles a couple of points off where it sits at rest when the tab bar is collapsed. The two positions the pill can occupy -- above the tab bar, or merged into it after scrolling -- don't sit the same way, and the landing now accounts for whichever one it is coming home to, worked out at the moment it closes rather than at the moment it opened.

- Shuffle and repeat work. Both buttons were drawn on the player and both were dead -- the queue had no notion of either, so enabling them would have been a control that lied about what it did. Shuffle now rearranges everything still to come and leaves the song playing alone, because pressing it was never a request to restart what you are listening to; pressing it again puts the original order back, carrying on from wherever you have got to rather than handing back songs you just heard. Repeat is one button with three positions -- off, the queue round again, this song round again -- and the glyph changes for the third, since a tinted "repeat" and a tinted "repeat.1" would otherwise be the same control describing two different behaviours. Both switches survive closing the app, and both are now on the lock screen and in CarPlay, showing the position the player is actually in.
- The Shuffle button on an album, a playlist or an artist turns the player's shuffle switch on instead of quietly handing over a pre-shuffled list. The old way left the switch reading off over a queue that was plainly shuffled, and no way back to the record's running order; now it lights up, and pressing it puts the album back into sequence from wherever you are in it. Which song opens is still drawn at random -- a shuffle that always starts on track one isn't one.
- Repeat All stops the queue gathering more music onto the end. The suggestions that keep an album playing past its last song are what a queue asked to come round again never gets to reach; the top-up is suspended while the button is on, and turning it off fills the queue straight back up.
- A playlist looks like a record rather than a list with a picture on top. The artwork is the size an album's cover is and blurs and dims out of the way at the same rate as you scroll, the playlist's name hands over to the top bar once the header's own has gone under it, and the songs are the artwork rows the rest of the app draws -- cover, title over artist, keep badge, duration -- rather than a row with a heart column stealing the width. Starring moved into the long press, where the album screen already keeps it.
- A playlist's songs answer to the same gestures an album's do: swipe right for Play Next, swipe left for Play Last, long press for the queue actions, starring and keep. The two screens shared none of that before, so which gesture did what depended on which screen you were standing on.

- The accent colour and the language can be set inside the app when it is running in a container like LiveContainer. Those two preferences live in Settings.app on a build iOS installed -- the accent in the app's own settings page, the language in the per-app picker iOS offers -- and an app running as a guest has no page there at all, so both rows led nowhere. A guest now gets the pickers in Settings itself, and a build installed on the device keeps the rows it always had. The app's own text changes language immediately; anything iOS draws for us, like the share sheet, follows the next time the app is opened.
- Artists browse as a grid of round covers in lettered sections, with the index strip down the side to jump between them and the current letter in the top bar -- the same screen albums already had, so the library reads the same way whichever half of it you are in. Artist names no longer come out tinted in the accent colour.
- The download and settings buttons in the top bar sit in one glass capsule instead of two. Two capsules meant the gap between them was the bar's to decide, which is what left the arrow floating well off the gear, and the sync spinner never quite landed between its neighbours.
- The top bar's download button says when something is actually being transferred: the arrow fills with the accent colour from tail to head, pauses, and does it again. It reports that a file is moving right now, which the screen behind the button says nothing about until it is opened.
- A long press on the gear while the library is syncing offers to stop the sync, rather than the only way to it being a trip into Settings.
- Pulling down on an artist's banner stretches it from the top of the screen rather than opening a gap above it, the seam that could appear along the bottom edge mid-flick is gone, and the refresh spinner sits under the navigation bar where it belongs instead of behind the status bar.

- Settings is a short screen of destinations rather than one long list. The server card is now the way into everything about the server -- what was connected, the custom headers, the Library and its syncs, and scrobbling -- and Playback, Accessibility and Storage each get a screen of their own. Nothing was removed; what changed is that the top of Settings can be taken in at a glance instead of scrolled through to find the one row you came for.
- Downloads have no size limit any more. The old cap was a number picked in Settings that silently stopped a keep part way through an album, and the only sign of it was music that never arrived. What someone deliberately asked to carry is now bounded by the device, the same as any other file on it -- and the size limit that remains governs only the cache the app fills by itself.
- Downloads live in Storage, next to the space they take, rather than at the bottom of Playback. The section says how many songs are on the device and how much room they use, keeps the format, quality and "over Cellular" controls, and adds a Delete All Downloads that asks first: it empties the downloads, cancels anything still on its way, and says as much before it does it.
- The Storage meter counts the cache alone. It used to add the downloads into the same figure, so the bar showed space that clearing the cache could not recover -- and went on showing it afterwards, since clearing never touched the downloads. The two are now separate numbers, and clearing the cache leaves the first one reading zero.
- What is waiting to download is part of the Downloaded screen instead of a screen of its own, listed under what is already here -- the two answer the same question a beat apart. The way there now sits in the top bar at all times rather than appearing only while a transfer is running, so it can be found before starting one and doesn't vanish under the last song to land.
- An album's name hands over to the top bar as its cover scrolls away, instead of standing in the bar and in the header at the same time -- the same handoff the artist screen already made.

- Keeping a whole album is a button on the album screen rather than an entry inside its ellipsis menu, sitting beside the heart where starring already is. A menu hid both the action and its answer: whether the record was already kept took two taps to find out. The button says it in its own shape -- outline for a record that isn't kept, filled and green for one that is -- and while a keep is running it becomes the progress ring for it, so the "3 of 12" that used to appear as a line under the album title no longer pushes the whole track list down and back up again as it comes and goes.
- The ellipsis menu on the Now Playing screen does what its items say again. The menu opened, but pressing anything in it did nothing at all. The screen redraws ten times a second to move the playhead, and that redraw was reaching the open menu and rebuilding it under the finger, which loses the press. The parts of the screen that move with the clock and the parts that don't are now separated, so the menu stands still while it is open -- and the rest of the screen does less work per tick besides.
- The album cover softens as the track list rises over it instead of shrinking. The old shrink moved everything underneath it -- title, artist, buttons, the whole list slid up as the artwork got smaller, while you were reading it. The cover now keeps its size and blurs and dims out of the way, so nothing on the screen changes position but the scroll itself.
- The artist screen's banner is a proper header: taller, with the picture drifting slower than the list travelling over it, blurring and fading as the name written across it goes, and the artist's name arriving in the top bar as it does. Pulling down past the top stretches the picture rather than exposing the background behind it.

- A song waiting to be downloaded on a slow connection starts playing a third of the way in again, instead of after all of it. The app feeds the player out of the file as it fills, and on a slow link every read was being answered with only the bytes that had arrived so far -- which says "the song ends here" to the player, so it gave up on a song that was still coming. The app read that as a song the phone couldn't decode, dropped the download and went back to streaming over the same bad connection, which is exactly what the download was avoiding. Reads now wait for the bytes they asked for.
- A connection judged too slow stays judged that way until it proves otherwise, rather than until a timer runs out. The verdict used to expire on its own, so the app went back to streaming over a link nothing had said was better, discovered it wasn't, and started over -- a song at a time. It now lifts only on evidence: sustained speed over the bar the current quality needs, no failures for a while. The verdict also survives closing the app, so a relaunch in the same tunnel doesn't rediscover it the hard way.
- The song already playing moves off a stream the moment the connection is judged unfit, picking up at the second it left off. That rule was only ever applied when a song was loaded, so the song that produced the evidence went on streaming over the link its own readings had just condemned, until it died.
- The next song is fetched at the bitrate the connection actually managed rather than the one in Settings. After the current song stepped down to 64 kbps to arrive at all, the song behind it was still being asked for at 192 -- five megabytes over a link doing twenty-five kilobytes a second, arriving seconds before it was needed, and a miss there means a gap between songs and another wait at the start of the next one.
- Settings gains "Adjust Quality Automatically", in Playback beneath the quality and transcode rows. On, the quality chosen is a request: a connection too slow for it gets a smaller copy so the song arrives at all, replaced with the real thing the next time it plays on a good connection. Off, it is exact, and a song on a bad connection may take a very long time to start or never arrive -- both positions are spelled out under the switch, because that is not something a five-word label can carry.
- Kept music is browsed by album. The Downloaded screen shows a shelf of kept album covers, like the Home screen's carousels, with the full grid a tap away on the headline; kept songs the server files under no album stay as rows beneath it rather than dropping off the screen.
- The badge on a track row is green when the copy is kept and grey when it is merely cached, so the two say different things at a glance rather than differing only in weight -- one is a copy the app is holding and will evict in its own time, the other is one that was asked for and stays.
- "Stop Keeping" now deletes the copy instead of handing it to the automatic cache. A kept song is not necessarily one that was ever played, so leaving it behind kept the space taken -- and the badge showing -- long after it was given back. The exception is the song playing at the time, which is only unpinned: deleting the file out from under the player is not what was asked for.
- The Now Playing screen says whether there is a copy of the song on the device, in the same line that carries its year and genre.
- A lossless song stored on the device is repacked correctly whatever its bit depth or channel count. FLAC allows depths the destination format doesn't, and those are now carried in the next size up rather than trimmed to fit -- padding is lossless, truncating is not -- while anything beyond stereo is repacked with the channel layout the encoder needs to be told about.

- Songs, albums and playlists can be kept on the device, so they stay playable with no server and no connection. "Keep" sits on every track row, in the Now Playing menu and on an album's or playlist's ellipsis menu; "Stop Keeping" hands the copy back to the ordinary cache, which is free to evict it again. Kept copies are fetched in their own format and quality -- a new Downloads section in Playback Settings, with a size limit of its own -- on Wi-Fi only unless told otherwise, and always behind whatever playback is fetching, so keeping an album never slows down the song being listened to.
- The badge on a track row now says which of four things is true rather than just "on the device or not": queued, arriving (with its progress), kept, or cached from having been played. The Downloaded screen separates what was deliberately kept from what happens to be cached, and each half plays as its own queue.
- What is waiting to be downloaded has a screen of its own, listing the queue in the order it will arrive, with the transfer in flight showing its progress, "Waiting for Wi-Fi" where that is what's holding it up, and cancelling per song or all at once. It is reachable from the top bar of every browse screen for as long as anything is queued -- keep an album, carry on browsing, and the way back to the queue follows you -- and disappears once everything has landed.

- Dragging the progress bar in a song stored on the device as Opus now lands where you drop it. iOS cannot seek an Opus file: it has no way to find a moment in one, so it divides the file up by an assumed bitrate and picks a spot from that -- which on these files was out by several percent, enough that dragging near the end of a song landed past the end of the audio and skipped straight to the next one. The app now finds the moment itself, by reading the timing the file records for each of its pages, and hands iOS a stream that begins exactly there. Nothing is re-downloaded and nothing on the server is touched; the whole thing happens on the device against the copy already there. Songs still arriving over the network were never affected -- those are seeked by asking the server to start the song where you dropped the scrubber.
- Songs stored as Opus no longer report the length of the song before them. Where one song ran into the next without a gap, the app measured the wrong file and gave the new song its predecessor's length. Two ways that was heard: a song shown shorter than it is ran its clock past a total sitting at 0:00, and a song shown longer put the end of the progress bar past the end of the audio -- so dragging near it skipped the song instantly, and the crossfade, which is timed against that same length, never got the chance to start.
- The Now Playing line no longer claims a song is streaming after you drag the progress bar. Seeking a song stored on the device left it reading "Stream", and the codec and bitrate beside it described what the connection would have asked for rather than the copy actually playing.

- A song whose stream quietly stops arriving no longer plays into silence. A connection that drops mid-song doesn't fail in any way the app could see -- the player holds a perfectly good song and is simply never fed again -- so the music stopped, the pause button went on claiming to play, and nothing happened until you pressed something. The app now watches for exactly that (no sound while bytes have stopped landing) and picks the song back up from the second it stopped: it fetches the rest of it from there, plays that from the device, and only falls back to fetching the whole song again where the server can't start part way through. Where the song was already fully downloaded, it just carries on from the file.
- The app recovers from the system's media services restarting, instead of needing to be closed and reopened. When iOS resets the media system underneath an app, every player it holds is dead: each song afterwards failed instantly, the buffering wait restarted over and over, and the only way back was relaunching. The app now rebuilds its players when that happens -- prompted by the system's own notice of it, and by recognising the failure -- and returns to where you were listening.
- A song the phone refuses to decode is no longer mistaken for a bad connection. That refusal was being counted as the link failing, which downloaded every following song before playing it and asked the server for a lower bitrate each time, walking down to the lowest one there is -- on a connection that was moving megabytes a second and fetching the next songs at full quality without trouble. Failures are now told apart by what actually caused them: only the ones a network produces count against the connection. A song that won't decode is retried a different way instead, and only then at a different encoding, since each one is a separately encoded file rather than the same one quieter.
- On a genuinely slow connection, the quality drops to something that will actually arrive, in one step. The wait for the first sound used to come down one rung at a time, each rung costing a slow transfer to discover: on a capped mobile connection that meant minutes of spinner while the app learned what one calculation answers. It now measures how fast the song is really arriving and picks the bitrate that has the music playing within about twelve seconds -- straight from 320 to 96 if that is what the link can do. The quality you chose is still what it asks for first; this only happens when that proves too slow, and the smaller copy is replaced by the real one the next time the song plays on a good connection.
- Songs are no longer fetched twice at once on a bad connection. The song being waited on and the lookahead fetching the same song could run side by side, each getting half of a link that was already struggling.
- A transfer that stops part way through is now noticed in twenty seconds rather than sixty, without punishing a server that takes its time starting -- the wait for the first byte and a gap in the middle of a transfer are judged separately.
- The bitrate shown for a stream is the bitrate you're getting. Choosing a codec on a connection that was previously set to send the original file left "Lossless" behind as its ceiling, which asked the server for a transcode with no limit at all, filed the saved copy under a quality it isn't, and left the Now Playing line with nothing to show -- while Settings displayed something else entirely.
- The length shown for a song streamed as Opus is no longer replaced by the phone's guess at it. A stream the phone can't measure gets an estimate worked out from an assumed bitrate, and adopting that dragged the end of the song forward with it -- starting the next track somewhere in the middle of the current one. The decoded length is now taken only where it can be measured, which is when the song is a complete file on the device.

- The library is kept on the device, so browsing it no longer waits on the server -- or needs one. Every browse screen -- albums, artists, songs, genres, playlists, favourites -- used to ask the server for its contents each time it opened, which meant a wait on a slow connection and an empty screen on none at all. They now read a local index of the whole library instead: the albums grid pages through it in the time a single request used to take, the alphabet strip lands instantly wherever it is dragged, and all of it works in a tunnel. Search answers from the index first and then lets the server improve the answer if it can, rather than showing nothing until the request comes back. The index is filled by a full sync -- resumable, so an interrupted one carries on where it stopped rather than starting over -- and kept current by a quick sync that runs when the app opens. Settings gains a Library section showing how many songs are indexed and when it last synced, with buttons to run either sync and to cancel one in progress; a spinner joins the settings gear on every screen while a sync runs, and pulling down on a browse screen asks for a quick sync. Until the library has been downloaded once, browse screens say so and offer to download it, instead of showing a blank grid that reads like an empty library. Logging out clears the index -- it belongs to one server and one account.
- Cover art seen once is kept on disk, so a browsed library still looks like one after the app has been closed, and offline. Nothing is prefetched: what is kept is what was actually looked at, and a song's own cover falls back to its album's when it can't be fetched. The pictures get a size cap of their own -- "Max Cover Art Size" in Settings, 256 MB by default -- rather than a share of the storage budget, because covers and downloaded songs sit on the same disk and browsing the library should never be able to evict music somebody asked to keep.
- A bad-connection verdict no longer follows you onto a different network. The app remembers a link it has judged unfit across launches, so a relaunch on the same bad connection doesn't rediscover it the hard way -- but the verdict was remembered as a deadline alone, with nothing saying which connection it was about, so a judgement earned on cellular in a tunnel carried on into the Wi-Fi at home and kept preloading and transcoding there for the rest of its hold. The verdict is now stamped with the link it was formed on and dropped the moment the app is on a different one, along with every measurement taken behind it.
- A server that won't serve cover art is no longer mistaken for a bad connection. The speed check downloads a cover and times it; a server answering "no such cover" was counted the same as no answer at all -- so a library whose covers the server declines ended up permanently judged unfit, downloading and transcoding every song on a connection that was never anything but fine. A refusal that arrives promptly over the very link being judged is now read as what it is: an answer, and no evidence against the connection.

- Long song titles scroll instead of being cut off. A title, album or artist wider than the space it has now holds at its start, travels to its end, waits there, and comes back -- in the mini player, in the pill the player shrinks to, and on the Now Playing screen, where all three lines move as one block rather than each drifting at its own pace. Lines that fit still sit still, and with Reduce Motion on nothing moves at all. Long titles are the norm on this screen -- classical movements, remix credits, multi-artist billings -- and it is the screen you opened to read what is playing, so an ellipsis was the wrong answer on any of them.
- The mini player gives the song's name the whole row it was already occupying. The title used to stop a quarter of the way short of the play button with nothing but empty space between, however long it was: the row split its free width evenly between the title and the gap in front of the controls. The title now claims that width itself, and the play and skip buttons sit as one pair against the pill's edge instead of drifting apart with the row's spacing between them.
- The Settings server row no longer carries a blue circle with a music note in it. The row says which server you are on; the badge said nothing the row didn't.

- The Now Playing song info line says where the music is coming from in a single word: "Cache" for a copy on the device, "Stream" for one arriving live, in place of the longer "Cached" and "Streaming". Same meaning, less of the line spent on it, so the codec and bitrate beside it stay readable.

- A bad connection no longer ends in silence with no way back. The app now health-checks the connection continuously: a ping and a small timed download against your own server when the app starts, every time it returns to the foreground, and on a rolling interval in between, alongside speed measurements taken off the transfers it is already making -- so a link too slow to stream is known *before* the first song is asked to survive it, not learned from its failure. The moment the link looks unfit -- slow pings, measured speed below what streaming needs, a playback failure or a pair of timeouts -- it stops handing the player live streams that can't survive it, and the verdict is remembered across launches. On a connection judged bad, each song is downloaded ahead of playing: the buffering indicator sits in the Now Playing screen's year-and-genre line, the download fills the seek bar as a faint pulsing layer behind the playhead, and the music starts once a third of the song is on the device -- the rest keeps downloading underneath while it plays. If playback catches up with the download, it pauses and shows buffering again until the file is comfortably ahead, with the play button held (no timeout -- skipping always works) whenever sound is held. The download retries on its own for as long as you leave the song waiting -- and every failed attempt immediately asks the next one for a lower bitrate, down to an emergency floor below anything Settings offers, because on a link that bad the smaller song is the one that arrives. The song info line reads "Loading" for the whole transfer and names the codec and bitrate actually being fetched -- not the Settings choice -- keeps naming them for the rest of the listen, and flips to "Cached" (never "Streaming") once the download completes mid-song. Downloads use the system's background transfer service where the install supports it (so they keep running while the app is suspended), fall back to in-process transfers where it doesn't -- sideloaded installs mostly don't -- and remember the answer, with the in-process path keeping going for a stretch after backgrounding and picking straight back up when you return. And recovery is deliberately hard to earn: a bad-connection verdict stands for at least three minutes however fast the bursts look, fast transfers only count once the link has gone two minutes without an actual failure, and a link that merely limps along keeps the verdict alive instead of quietly aging out of it -- so the *next* song on a still-bad connection is preloaded too, rather than handed to a stream that dies. The quality setting is treated as a target rather than a promise: a struggling link is asked for a bitrate it can actually carry -- stepped down as far as needed, judged from the measured speed -- and the smaller copy is upgraded automatically the next time the song plays on a healthy connection, the same way lesser cached copies always have been. A stream that dies mid-song recovers by itself, a downloaded copy that refuses to play is thrown away and fetched afresh instead of failing on every press, and the play button sits out the first stretch of a buffering wait -- dimmed, coming back after half a minute regardless. Songs already on the device play on a bad connection whatever quality they were saved at. Once songs move at full speed again, the app goes back to ordinary streaming by itself.
- On a bad connection the songs come first, the pictures after. While the current song -- and then the next ones, which keep prefetching on a bad connection precisely because the song playing is already on the device -- are being downloaded, cover art, lock-screen artwork and the queue's "more like this" lookups hold off rather than competing for a link that can barely carry one thing, and catch up the moment the songs are through. The rare playback error that still surfaces now speaks your language properly instead of quoting the system's one-line apology.
- The log now says what actually went wrong, and says it in English. A failure used to be written down as the one-line apology iOS composes in the device's language — "Vorgang kann nicht abgeschlossen werden", which names neither the operation nor why it couldn't be — while the error's real content, the code and the chain of causes underneath it, was thrown away. A playback failure on a bad connection now reads like "the operation could not be completed (AVErrorUnknown, see the underlying error) [AVFoundationErrorDomain -11800] -- caused by: the network connection was lost mid-transfer [NSURLErrorDomain -1005]", whatever language the phone is set to. Error banners in the app itself are unchanged and still speak your language; this is about the log you read and export under Settings → Diagnostics.

- Songs you listen to are kept, without being downloaded a second time. A song that wasn't already on the device used to be fetched twice over: once to play it, and once again, from the same server, to keep it — two transcodes of one song, racing each other. It cost enough that it was only ever done on Wi-Fi, so nothing you played on cellular was kept at all. The bytes that play the song are now written down as they arrive, so keeping it costs nothing beyond hearing it, and it happens on every connection.
- Songs stop breaking up mid-play and restarting from the beginning. When a stream stalled, iOS asked the server for it again — and a server transcoding as it sends can only answer by starting the song over, which was heard as the track jumping back to its beginning while the progress bar carried on regardless, every position wrong from then on. What has already arrived is now held on the device, so that second ask is answered from there instead of from the server.
- A song is only kept when the whole of it arrived. Skipping part way through, or scrubbing, leaves nothing behind rather than a partial file — a half-finished song still claims its full length, and once kept it would play out early or scrub to the wrong place every time. Nothing kept this way skips the checks a download goes through: it is verified against the length the server reports, and repacked so scrubbing lands exactly.

- Settings no longer says the version twice. The footer read "SwiftDrome 0.8.1 (0.8.1)" — the brackets are where iOS puts the build number, and there was nothing to put in them, so they only repeated what stood in front of them. The commit the build came from now sits there instead, on the same line rather than a line of its own: "SwiftDrome 0.8.2 (a1b2c3d)", or "(local)" for a build made on your own machine. The line is still selectable, to be pasted into a bug report.

- The logs can be read in the app. Settings → Diagnostics used to offer one thing, an export, which meant diagnosing anything on the device started by sending files to another app. That row now leads to the log itself: newest entries first, filterable by category and down to errors only, and searchable by text. A crash or a hang report sits at the top of the screen when there is one, and opens as the text it is. The export is still there, on the same screen, and still hands over everything — what you filtered the view down to never changes what gets sent.
- Rows that lead somewhere answer anywhere along them. Logs in Settings, and Playlists, Artists, Albums and the rest of the Library list, only reacted where something was drawn — the words and the chevron — so a tap in the space between them, or just above or below the text, did nothing at all. The whole row is the target now.
- Settings says which build is installed. Every preview build of a pull request carries the last release's version number, so two of them were indistinguishable once installed; the footer now shows the commit each build came from underneath the version, and reads "local" for a build made on your own machine. The line can be selected and copied straight into a bug report.

- Songs streamed as Opus can be downloaded again. Every Opus download was being thrown away the moment it finished, on the grounds that it had arrived incomplete — and it hadn't: iOS works an Opus file's length out from an assumed bitrate rather than reading the length the file states, and it was wrong by up to half a minute on a three-and-a-half-minute song. Nothing reached the device, so nothing could be played offline, and the app kept trying: the same song was fetched again a second later, and again, for as long as it was in the queue. An Opus file is now measured by what it says about itself, exact to the sample, and the check that rejects a genuinely truncated download is the file's own account of whether it ended.
- Scrubbing a song streamed as Opus now lands where you drop it. A server transcodes as it sends, so the stream has no length and no way to be asked for a position part way through — a scrub either settled back where playback already was or never arrived. The app now asks the server to start the song where you dropped the scrubber, which it can do because it is reading its own file, and covers the last fraction of a second itself. Landing is exact. Servers that don't support this are detected rather than assumed, and scrubbing behaves as it did before on them.
- The length shown for an Opus song is the song's, not an estimate. The progress bar could be built on a length several percent short of the audio — a three-minute song reported as two-fifty — which put every position, the remaining time and the end of the track out with it.
- A download that fails is no longer retried immediately, over and over. One that couldn't be fetched was being started again the instant it failed, roughly once a second for as long as the song stayed in the queue, and each attempt pulled the whole song down before being discarded. A failed download now waits five minutes, and the songs behind it in the queue are fetched in the meantime instead of being held up behind it.
- Scrubbing a lossless song now lands where you drop it. Dragging to 2:50 in a three-minute FLAC could start the audio nearly a minute earlier while the progress bar and the remaining time both insisted you were where you had asked to be — iOS works a FLAC's position out from an assumed bitrate instead of reading the seek table the file carries, so the further into a song you reached the further short it landed, and it reported the position you asked for either way. Downloaded songs are now kept in a container iOS can seek exactly: still lossless, still the same audio, and about the same size on disk. A song that is still streaming is fetched from the byte your seek points at, which lands within a tenth of a second. Nothing on the server is touched, re-encoded or renamed — this happens on the device, to the app's own copy.
- Reopening the app returns to where you left a lossless song, rather than to wherever the seek happened to land. The check meant to catch a restored position that missed was trusting a clock that reports the position it was asked for, so it never found anything to correct.
- A download that arrives incomplete no longer becomes a permanently broken song. Two ways a bad file used to end up in the cache looking like a good one: a server answering with an error page instead of the track, stored as if it were music, and a connection closing part-way through a transfer the app had no length to check it against. Either one is poison once cached — a half-finished FLAC still claims the full length in its header, so it plays out early, skips, or lands somewhere else every time you scrub. Downloads are now checked against the file size and length the server reports for the track, and anything short is discarded instead of kept.
- The app has a real icon. Installed builds used to sit on the home screen as a blank placeholder, because nothing in the build carried an icon at all; SwiftDrome now ships its own mark — two triangles for the outgoing and incoming track, with the overlap where both are audible drawn in its own lighter colour. The same mark greets you on the login screen in place of the stock music symbol, and the AltStore source now shows it as the app's icon and header rather than two broken images.

- The app can be installed and updated from the AltStore source again. Every build so far reported itself as version 1.0.0 no matter which release it was — the version was never written into the app, so the build tool filled in its own placeholder — and AltStore refuses to install an app whose version disagrees with the one the source advertises. Builds now carry their real version number, and the source lists the iOS version the app actually needs (26) rather than the 17 it was seeded with.
